rationale: B wins slightly because it keeps its hands cleaner: it labels what is company-stated, asks for proof before making the big claims, and refuses the IPO bait. A has the sharper extra market lens in "Figma Has 4 Million Users and Just Entered AI Code Generation," but it also wanders into unsourced story varnish like "first major product announcement" and "That's a different company than Adobe would have built." B's "Figma adds a $25 seat for AI design-to-code, on top of what teams already pay" is a plain, pitchable SaaS-pricing angle; boring in the useful way.
gaps_in_A: "first major product announcement as a fully independent company" is unsupported. The update only says the launch follows the Adobe collapse; it does not establish first or major.
"weeks away from being absorbed into Adobe" and "That's a different company than Adobe would have built" are narrative garnish, not supplied fact. Fine as a question, sloppy as asserted framing.
"The $25 'Make' Seat Tells You Exactly What Figma Is Selling Post-Adobe" overclaims the pricing read; the facts give a price, not a definitive strategy.
"no IPO timing disclosed" gets inflated into "a meaningful negative signal"; absence of timing is not an investor thesis without a source who will say it.
gaps_in_B: "shippable React code" is ahead of the evidence. The update says working front-end code; shippable is exactly what the proof has to establish.
"Figma's first move after the Adobe deal died" smuggles in 'first.' The facts say the launch follows the collapse, not that it is the first move or first notable push.
"category-creation" is too grand for this fact set. A tool exporting React may pressure a category, but category creation needs adoption, competitor movement, or buyer behavior evidence.
"three structurally distinct shapes exist" leaves out a real fourth shape: Figma's 4 million users and Fortune 500 reach as distribution pressure on prompt-to-UI and design-to-code rivals.
